subject: literature
passage: For a month, Ustad Rafiq did not let Bilal touch a brush. He sat the boy on a stool at the back of the Anarkali shop, among the drying signboards, and had him watch. Bilal watched the old man load the flat brush and lay down a curve of black Urdu lettering in one motion, as though the letter had always been there under the paint and he were only uncovering it. On the thirtieth day Rafiq handed him a board and a pot of paint and said nothing. Bilal's first stroke wobbled and thinned; his second was worse. Only then did he understand what he had been watching: not a trick of the hand but a month of decisions made so fast that they looked like none at all.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the signboards produced in a painter's shop in Lahore
choices.B: To criticize a teacher's refusal to explain his craft to a beginner
choices.C: To show that calligraphy can only be learned through imitation rather than instruction
choices.D: To portray an apprentice's realization of the skill concealed in his teacher's apparently effortless work

explanation.why: The text builds toward Bilal's realization in the last sentence. For a month the master's lettering looks effortless, as if he were "only uncovering" letters already there. When Bilal tries and fails, he understands that what looked like "a trick of the hand" was really many rapid decisions. The purpose is to portray that moment of understanding.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The signboards are background details; the text is about the apprentice and what he learns.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not judge Rafiq's silence negatively; his method is what produces Bilal's understanding.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text tells one apprentice's story and makes no general claim about how calligraphy must be learned.
explanation.D: Correct. Every detail leads to the final sentence, in which Bilal grasps what the month of watching had hidden: skill made of countless quick decisions.
